No — that sketch has a dangling-string_view bug, and it's exactly the red-flag case: "the caller will use it right away."

`result` is a local `std::string`. `std::string_view` does not own or copy anything; it is a pointer-plus-length into someone else's buffer. The moment `trim` returns, `result` is destroyed and the returned view points at freed stack memory. "Use it right away" doesn't help — the string's destructor already ran before the caller got control back. That's a use-after-free (or silent garbage if that stack slot gets reused) every single call.

Two ways to fix it, and the right one depends on the API contract you actually want:

**Option A — return an owning `std::string` (simplest, safest).**

```cpp
std::string trim(const std::string& input) {
  return strip_ws(input);
}
```

RVO makes this cheap; no dangling possible. If `strip_ws` already returns `std::string`, just `return strip_ws(input);` and let copy elision move it out. This is the default choice unless you have a measured reason to avoid the allocation.

**Option B — if you genuinely want a non-owning view, view into the *caller's* buffer, not a local.**

```cpp
std::string_view trim(std::string_view input) {
  const auto first = input.find_first_not_of(" \t\r\n");
  if (first == std::string_view::npos) return {};
  const auto last = input.find_last_not_of(" \t\r\n");
  return input.substr(first, last - first + 1);
}
```

This is safe because it returns a view into `input`, which the caller owns and which outlives the call. This is normally the *better* design — trimming needs no allocation at all. But note the contract change: it takes `std::string_view`, so it no longer accepts a temporary `std::string` safely either. `trim(make_string())` would dangle for the same reason. If you want both, provide the owning `std::string` overload (Option A) and document that the `string_view` overload requires the caller to keep the source alive.

A couple of things to check against the project before you land this:

- If `strip_ws` returns a `std::string` by value, Option A lets the compiler elide the copy — don't hand-write `std::string result = ...; return result;` where `return strip_ws(input);` suffices.
- Match the file's language: if this lands in a `.c` header's neighborhood or the project targets a pre-C++17 standard, `std::string_view` isn't available — use the owning `std::string` form.

For "the caller will use it right away," the honest reading is: the caller wants a value they can hold onto, so Option A is what you actually want. Option B is worth it only if you've confirmed the caller keeps the source buffer alive across the call and you're avoiding an allocation on a hot path.

Someone on the team says they fixed the reported heap-buffer-overflow in TokenStream::peek() by adding a bounds check. The plain `ctest --test-dir build` run is green. How do I actually confirm the fix is correct before we close the ticket?

trialRecords.output:
A green plain `ctest` run only tells you the fix didn't break existing behavior — it says nothing about whether the overflow is actually gone. A bounds check that "looks right by inspection" is exactly the class of change that can still be wrong (off-by-one in the comparison, checking the wrong buffer/length, checking after the dereference instead of before). Confirm it with a sanitizer run, not by reading the diff.

**1. Reproduce first, on the pre-fix revision.** Build the *unfixed* code under ASan+UBSan and run the test that exercises `peek()`:

```bash
cmake -S . -B build-asan -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS='-fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g'
cmake --build build-asan
ctest --test-dir build-asan --output-on-failure
```

You want to see the heap-buffer-overflow report on the pre-fix revision. If it doesn't reproduce there, you don't yet have a regression test that actually covers the bug — fix that before touching the report. Keep this build directory around; the pair of results is the evidence.

**2. Confirm the regression test exists and fails for the right reason.** The fix should come with a test case in the stream's test file (matching the project's existing fixture/assertion style) that drives `peek()` at the boundary — peeking at/just past the end of the buffer, an empty stream, a stream whose internal buffer is exactly one past capacity. Under the ASan build on the *buggy* revision it should blow up; under the same build on the fixed revision it must run clean. A green suite with no case that reaches the boundary is not verification.

**3. Re-run ASan on the fixed revision.** Same command as step 1 against the current tree. Both requirements: the whole suite passes, and the ASan binary prints no error report (no leak, no overflow, no UB message). "ctest green" and "ASan clean" are separate facts — capture both.

**4. Check for the adjacent bug the bounds check may have hidden.** `peek()` overflowing usually means a length/capacity invariant is wrong somewhere nearby, so extend coverage slightly: peek at the last valid index and at one-past-the-end, empty stream, stream that has been partially consumed then refilled, and (if a caller indexes off the returned reference) the caller path too. Run those under ASan as well. This is where a subtly wrong check — e.g. `<` where `<=` is needed — actually shows up.

**5. If `peek()` touches any shared state** (a refcounted buffer, a cursor another thread reads, a pool), also build and run under TSan in a *separate* configuration — ASan/UBSan and TSan can't share a binary:

```bash
cmake -S . -B build-tsan -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS='-fsanitize=thread -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g'
cmake --build build-tsan && ctest --test-dir build-tsan --output-on-failure
```

And make sure any test that spawns a thread joins it before asserting — no `sleep`-based synchronization, which would make the result non-deterministic anyway.

**How to report it when all of the above hold:**

```
Generated: tests/token_stream_test.cpp
  - N cases (fixture/assertion style matching the existing file), ctest all passing
  - Boundary cases for peek(): empty stream, last valid index, one-past-end,
    partial-consume-then-refill
  - Regression case reproduced the heap-buffer-overflow under ASan on the
    pre-fix revision; passes clean under ASan+UBSan on the fixed revision
```

If ASan still reports anything on the fixed revision — including a report from a *different* line than before — the ticket stays open; a bounds check that moves the overflow rather than removing it is a common failure mode here. Note also that only test files were changed by you; if the fix itself turns out to be wrong, say so rather than editing production code silently.

Bottom line: don't close the ticket on `ctest` green. Close it on a reproduced-before / clean-after pair of ASan+UBSan runs, with a boundary-reaching regression test that exists in the suite.

A green plain `ctest` run is not evidence the heap-buffer-overflow is fixed — a bounds check that "looks right" is exactly the class of change that can be wrong by one, off by an edge case, or mask the overflow at one call site while leaving another unguarded, and none of that shows up without a sanitizer. Here is how to actually confirm it before closing the ticket.

## 1. Get the reproduction case in hand

Before trusting any fix, confirm there's a test that reproduced the original overflow — a heap-buffer-overflow means something read or wrote one element past the end of a heap allocation, so the regression test has to drive `TokenStream::peek()` to that boundary (peek at the last valid position, then at/just past the end, and on an empty or just-exhausted stream). If the "fix" landed without such a test, that's the first thing missing: the ticket shouldn't close without a test that fails on the pre-fix revision.

## 2. Verify the regression test fails on the pre-fix code

This is the step people skip. Stash the fix (or check out the pre-fix revision), build with ASan, and run the new test. It must fail *with an ASan report that names the same overflow in `TokenStream::peek()`*. A test that passes both before and after proves nothing — it never exercised the bug. Capture that ASan stack trace; it's your baseline.

## 3. Rebuild with ASan+UBSan and run the whole suite

Plain ctest almost certainly used a normal build. Build a separate sanitizer configuration:

```bash
cmake -S . -B build-asan -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS='-fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g'
cmake --build build-asan
ctest --test-dir build-asan --output-on-failure
```

The regression test must now run clean — no ASan report at all, not just "no failure exit". If the test asserts a specific value but ASan still fires, that's not fixed. Run the *entire* suite in this build, not just the one test, because a bounds check added at one site can leave a sibling call path (a different overload, a `peek(n)`, an iterator path) still over-reading.

If any test touches shared concurrent state, that's a separate runtime — build and run a TSan configuration too (ASan/UBSan and TSan cannot coexist in one binary):

```bash
cmake -S . -B build-tsan -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS='-fsanitize=thread -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g'
cmake --build build-tsan && ctest --test-dir build-tsan --output-on-failure
```

## 4. Inspect the fix against the actual boundary, not the reported symptom

Read the bounds check and confirm it's correct at the edges, independent of whether tests pass:

- Off-by-one: does it allow index `== size`? `peek()` on a just-exhausted stream is the classic case — is reading "one past logical end" intended (a sentinel) or a bug?
- Empty stream: does the check handle `size() == 0` before any arithmetic?
- Signed/unsigned: comparisons between an index and `size()` where one side is signed can pass a check that doesn't actually bound the access — this is also why UBSan's signed-overflow checks matter here.
- Other accessors: if `peek()` is fixed but `next()`/`at()`/`operator*` share the same underlying read, the same overflow may live there.

A check that returns a sentinel instead of overflowing is only correct if every caller treats that sentinel as "no token" — verify the callers, don't assume.

## 5. Close the ticket with evidence

Report: the pre-fix ASan stack trace, the post-fix clean ASan+UBSan run of the full suite, the regression test path and what it drives, and (if threads were involved) the clean TSan run. Confirm all threads a test starts are joined before assertions, and no test synchronizes with a bare `sleep`. If the source fix was correct but no regression test exists, that's an open action item, not a closed ticket — the next change can reintroduce the same overflow with nothing to catch it.

Join the thread explicitly — or, if you want to assert while it's running, wait on a condition variable / future. Never `sleep`. Since you already have a `std::thread`, the direct answer is `join()` before the assertions:

```cpp
TEST_F(QueueProcessorTest, DrainsQueueBeforeStopping) {
  std::thread worker([this] { processor_.RunUntilStopped(); });

  for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i) queue_.push(i);
  processor_.Stop();          // signals the worker to finish the queue and exit

  worker.join();              // blocks until the thread has fully returned

  EXPECT_TRUE(queue_.empty());
  EXPECT_EQ(processed_.load(), 10);
}
```

A few things that matter as much as the `join()` itself:

**Signal the stop before joining.** `join()` blocks until the thread's function returns, so if the worker runs `while (!stop_requested_)`, nothing will unblock it and your test hangs forever. Make sure `Stop()` (or an equivalent) flips the flag and wakes the worker — typically via a condition variable, not a spin on an atomic.

**If you'd rather not build a stop flag, use a future.** `std::async` + `future::get()` gives you join-with-a-return-value in one step:

```cpp
auto fut = std::async(std::launch::async, [this] { return processor_.Drain(queue_); });
EXPECT_EQ(fut.get(), 10);   // get() blocks until the task completes
EXPECT_TRUE(queue_.empty());
```

**Don't fall back to a sleep.** `std::this_thread::sleep_for(100ms)` before asserting is the usual mistake here — it's non-deterministic under a loaded CI machine and will flake. `join()`, `future::get()`, or a `condition_variable::wait` with a predicate are the deterministic waits.

```bash
  -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS='-fsanitize=thread -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g'
cmake --build build-tsan && ctest --test-dir build-tsan --output-on-failure
```
